name: Bearchild v. Cobban
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Montana, Chief District Judge Dana L. Christensen)
topic: Sexual assault by prison staff as an Eighth Amendment violation, the line between an invasive pat search and an assault, and the jury instruction that misstated the elements
summary: A Montana State Prison inmate alleged that a sergeant turned a pat-down search on the way to a GED class into a five-minute groping, then had him pull his waistband away and stared while other guards laughed. The jury was given the standard Eighth Amendment excessive force instruction and found for the sergeant. The Ninth Circuit reversed and defined the claim: a prisoner proves an Eighth Amendment violation by showing that a staff member, without legitimate penological justification, touched the prisoner in a sexual manner or engaged in sexual conduct for the staff member's own gratification or to humiliate, degrade, or demean the prisoner. No force and no injury are required, and malice is presumed once a sexual assault is proved. It is the custody case that draws the line between a lawful invasive search and an assault.
coverage: The opinion, including Judge Callahan's partial concurrence and partial dissent and all footnotes, was read in full from the Ninth Circuit's own archive at https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2020/01/16/17-35616.pdf. The slip opinion carries docket No. 17-35616 and district court No. 6:14-cv-00012-DLC, was argued and submitted April 12, 2019 in Seattle, and was filed January 16, 2020. The panel was Judges W. Fletcher, Callahan, and Christen, with Judge Christen writing.

The slip opinion does not print its own Federal Reporter citation. The citation 947 F.3d 1130 appears in the public case listings that index this docket number and date (Justia and CourtListener); it was not confirmed from a reporter volume. Pin cites are not given because the slip opinion uses slip page numbers, not reporter pages.

The district court record, the trial transcript, the PREA investigation reports, and any proceedings after remand were not read. The facts are stated as the two opinions describe them, including where the majority and the dissent read the testimony differently.
Schwenk v. Hartford, 204 F.3d 1187 (9th Cir. 2000), and Wood v. Beauclair, 692 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2012), are described as this opinion describes them; they were not read separately for this brief.
facts:
The facts were disputed at trial and are given as the Ninth Circuit described them.

On the morning of November 4, 2013, Dewayne Bearchild and other Montana State Prison inmates walked from their housing unit to a general equivalency degree class in another part of the prison. Along the way, guards stopped Bearchild and another inmate for pat-down searches. Bearchild alleged that Sergeant Larry Pasha's pat-down "lasted about five minutes and involved rubbing, stroking, squeezing, and groping in intimate areas," that Pasha then ordered him to pull his waistband away from his body, "stared at his penis, and asked, 'Is that all of you?'" and that Pasha and the other guards watching "began laughing." Inmate James Ball, who was present, testified at trial to an account the court called "generally consistent with Bearchild's version of events," and testified that after watching the first part of the search he told guards "that's not right" and was "told to shut up." Bearchild testified that Pasha started the pat-down from behind and then moved in front of him; Ball testified the search began with Pasha behind Bearchild and was not asked whether Pasha moved to the front.

Pasha "vigorously disputed" that account, denied the search lasted five minutes or went beyond a permissible pat-down, and presented witnesses who explained that institutional security requires invasive procedures because inmates hide contraband in intimate areas knowing officers may be reluctant to look there. He demonstrated the scope of the search he said he conducted, using another prison employee as a stand-in. The dissent adds, from the trial record, that Pasha and Officer Schlosser both testified that Pasha felt a strange bulge in Bearchild's waistband during the initial pat-down, which prompted a focused follow-on search of the waist and groin, that Pasha had Bearchild pull his waistband away so he could look for contraband, and that the pat-down lasted only a few seconds. Bearchild's own testimony was that his penis was caught in his waistband after a hurried bathroom visit, that Pasha felt it from behind and asked "What is this?", came around to the front, "grabs this underneath. He is squeezing. Then he's rubbing this way," and then had him pull his pants and underwear away from his body to look inside.

The inmates' GED teacher, Sara Simmons, saw the first part of the search but did not testify. In two written statements she said her view was limited, that she saw Pasha ask Bearchild to pull his pants away from his waist, that she left until the search ended, and that Bearchild seemed upset afterward and told her the search was "not right." Bearchild filed a grievance the same day. A lieutenant conducted a Prison Rape Elimination Act investigation, concluded the search complied with prison procedure, and found "no basis" for the sexual assault allegation. Bearchild sued under 42 U.S.C. section 1983. The district court dismissed every defendant except Pasha, denied Pasha summary judgment on qualified immunity, and Bearchild, representing himself, tried the case to a six-member jury in July 2017. Eight PREA investigation reports about similar allegations against Pasha by other inmates were admitted under seal. The jury was given Instruction No. 12, drawn almost verbatim from Ninth Circuit Model Civil Jury Instruction 9.26, which required Bearchild to prove that Pasha "used excessive and unnecessary force under all of the circumstances," that he "acted maliciously and sadistically for the purpose of causing harm, and not in a good faith effort to maintain or restore discipline," and that his act "caused harm to the plaintiff," and which listed the extent of injury, the need to use force, and the relationship between the need and the amount of force among the factors to consider. A separate instruction, No. 13, requested by Pasha to give context to the PREA reports, gave one PREA regulatory definition of "sexual abuse." Bearchild did not object to any instruction. The jury returned a verdict for Pasha. With pro bono counsel, Bearchild appealed.
holding:
Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for a new trial. The panel first held that the district court did not abuse its discretion by failing to continue the trial on its own motion so that Bearchild could subpoena the GED teacher; the court had ordered two inmate witnesses produced by video, the teacher's written statements were available without objection, and Bearchild had said he wanted to go forward.

The rule. Because there was no model instruction for an Eighth Amendment sexual assault claim, the court "take[s] this opportunity to address our circuit's law governing this type of claim." It placed prisoner sexual assault claims within the excessive force framework of Hudson v. McMillian, then drew three points from Schwenk v. Hartford and Wood v. Beauclair: "First, sexual assault serves no valid penological purpose." "Second, where an inmate can prove that a prison guard committed a sexual assault, we presume the guard acted maliciously and sadistically for the very purpose of causing harm, and the subjective component of the Eighth Amendment claim is satisfied." "Finally, our cases have clearly held that an inmate need not prove that an injury resulted from sexual assault in order to maintain an excessive force claim under the Eighth Amendment," and "[a]ny sexual assault is objectively 'repugnant to the conscience of mankind' and therefore not de minimis for Eighth Amendment purposes." The court then announced the definition: "We now hold that a prisoner presents a viable Eighth Amendment claim where he or she proves that a prison staff member, acting under color of law and without legitimate penological justification, touched the prisoner in a sexual manner or otherwise engaged in sexual conduct for the staff member's own sexual gratification, or for the purpose of humiliating, degrading, or demeaning the prisoner." The court said the definition "recognizes that there are occasions when legitimate penological objectives within a prison setting require invasive searches" and "accounts for the significant deference courts owe to prison staff, who work in challenging institutional settings with unique security concerns." For a case like this one, "where the allegation is that a guard's conduct began as an invasive procedure that served a legitimate penological purpose, the prisoner must show that the guard's conduct exceeded the scope of what was required to satisfy whatever institutional concern justified the initiation of the procedure. Such a showing will satisfy the objective and subjective components of an Eighth Amendment claim."

The instruction. Measured against that law, Instruction No. 12 "misstated the elements necessary to establish liability for an Eighth Amendment violation arising from sexual assault" and "placed a greater burden on Bearchild than our law requires." The jury was told to find excessive and unnecessary force without being told that "any act constituting sexual assault is by definition both excessive and unnecessary"; told to find malicious and sadistic intent without being told that proof of sexual assault satisfies that element; and told to find that Pasha "caused harm," when the law does not require physical or lasting emotional injury. The factor on "the extent of the injury" "likely suggested that Bearchild was required to show the pat-down caused physical injury," and the factors on the need for force and the amount of force "likely confused the jury because it was unaccompanied by an explanation that sexual assault does not require violent physical force, or indeed, any force." The court reaffirmed "that sexual assault violates the Eighth Amendment regardless of the amount of force used." The PREA definition in Instruction No. 13 did not cure the problem: it was never tied to the Eighth Amendment claim, and because Instruction No. 11 told the jury to find for Pasha if any element of No. 12 was missing, the jury "may have decided there was no liability without ever reaching Instruction No. 13." Reviewing for plain error because Bearchild had not objected, the court found the error plain (an instruction that "adds an obviously non-existent element to the plaintiff's burden of proof"), prejudicial (Bearchild "introduced evidence from which a jury could have found that Pasha stroked and fondled him for the purpose of causing humiliation or for Pasha's own sexual gratification"), and a serious impairment of the fairness of the proceeding. The causation instruction, No. 10, was not plain error. The court added that Pasha could defend a retrial "in exactly the same way he did: by arguing that his pat-down search was not an unconstitutional sexual assault, and was instead a necessarily invasive but permissible pat-down for contraband."
dissent: Judge Callahan concurred on the continuance and dissented on the instruction. She agreed that "there is no penological justification for a prison guard to sexually assault a prisoner, and that if a plaintiff proves a sexual assault occurred then he or she necessarily has met the elements of an excessive force claim," and called the majority's definition "a correct statement of law but inapplicable to the factual dispute at issue in this case," because Pasha never argued that sexual abuse falls outside the Eighth Amendment; he argued there was no sexual assault, only a lawful search extended after he felt a suspicious lump. In her view the model instruction, read with the PREA definition in Instruction No. 13, "accurately (if imperfectly)" reflected Schwenk and Wood, so any error was not plain, and Bearchild could not show prejudice: his own testimony about the waistband "corroborated Pasha's defense," his eyewitness "diverged in material respects," the PREA investigator's report corroborated Pasha, and "even if the jury had been instructed more precisely on the relationship between sexual abuse and excessive force, it still would not have assigned liability to Pasha." She warned that it was "unclear" whether the new definition is to be woven into the excessive force instruction or to replace Model Instruction 9.26, which "will sow confusion in the district courts." The majority answered in a footnote that its task was to decide the appeal, not rewrite the model instructions, and that trial judges "must adapt instructions to accommodate the claims actually raised."
notDecided: Whether Pasha sexually assaulted Bearchild. The jury's verdict was set aside for an instructional error; the court made no finding on what happened during the search and sent the case back for a new trial under correct instructions. The dissent would have affirmed the verdict for Pasha. Qualified immunity was not before the panel; the district court had denied it before trial and the appeal was from the verdict. The court did not hold that Model Instruction 9.26 is wrong in other cases and did not write a replacement instruction. The lawfulness of a clothed pat search of the groin, or of having an inmate pull a waistband away so an officer can look inside, was not decided; the court assumed such searches can be required by legitimate penological objectives and treated the question as whether the conduct exceeded what the institutional concern required. Proceedings after remand were not researched for this brief.
inPractice: For custody staff, Bearchild draws the line between a search and an assault, and the line is scope and purpose, not force or injury. The court assumed that legitimate security needs can require an invasive clothed search, including the groin and waistband, because inmates hide contraband where officers hesitate to look. What takes a search across the line is conduct that "exceeded the scope of what was required to satisfy whatever institutional concern justified the initiation of the procedure," done "for the staff member's own sexual gratification, or for the purpose of humiliating, degrading, or demeaning the prisoner." Three things follow. First, the usual force defenses do not apply. Once a jury finds a sexual assault, malice is presumed, no injury is needed, and the amount of force is irrelevant, because "sexual assault violates the Eighth Amendment regardless of the amount of force used." An officer cannot argue that it was brief, that it was over the clothing, or that the inmate was not hurt. Second, the facts that decide these cases are the facts around the search: why it started (the waistband bulge), how long it lasted, what the officer said, who was present, and whether anyone laughed or commented. The dissent credited Pasha largely because an officer witness, the PREA investigator's report, and Bearchild's own account of the waistband supported a legitimate reason for the extended search; the majority sent the case back largely because an inmate witness heard "that's not right" and "told to shut up." Third, the PREA investigation and the lawsuit run on different tracks. The investigator found the search within policy and "no basis" for the complaint, and that finding did not end the civil case. The PREA definition of sexual abuse, "intentional contact, either directly or through the clothing of or with the genitalia, anus, groin, breast, inner thigh, or the buttocks that is unrelated to official duties or where the staff member has the intent to abuse, arouse, or gratify sexual desire," is the standard staff are trained to and the one a jury will hear alongside the constitutional one. Supervisors should read the eight sealed PREA reports in this case as the warning they are: prior complaints against the same officer were admitted at trial as public records.
trainIt: Teach the search before the law. Have students state the institutional reason for a clothed pat search, the areas it covers, how long it takes, and what changes when an officer feels something in a waistband or groin. Then teach the Bearchild rule against that baseline: the search is lawful as far as the security concern requires, and an assault begins where conduct exceeds that scope and serves gratification or humiliation. Run the Bearchild facts as a decision exercise. An inmate's hurried bathroom visit leaves a bulge at the waistband; the officer feels it from behind. Ask what the officer does next, who else should be present, what the officer says, and how the follow-on search is explained and ended. Then ask what the inmate's witness and the teacher who walked away will say about it. Teach narration and silence. The remark "Is that all of you?" and the laughter were the facts that made this a sexual assault allegation rather than a search complaint, and an inmate who said "that's not right" was "told to shut up." Train officers to say nothing about an inmate's body and to treat a bystander's objection as a reason to slow down and document, not to silence. Teach the two definitions together. The PREA definition of staff sexual abuse is already in every custody officer's training; show students that the Ninth Circuit's constitutional definition reaches the same conduct, that no injury or force is required under either, and that a PREA finding of "no basis" does not decide the civil case. Teach the record. In this case the officer's defense rested on a second officer's testimony about the bulge, the investigator's report, and the demonstration of the search procedure. An extended search of a sensitive area should be documented the same day with the reason, the duration, the staff present, and what was found.
caution: The opinion was read from the Ninth Circuit's slip opinion, so pin cites to 947 F.3d are not given, and the reporter citation itself comes from public case listings rather than from the opinion. The facts were contested at trial and the majority and dissent read the testimony differently; the brief gives both. The court decided a jury instruction question and announced a definition; it did not find that an assault occurred, and the dissent would have affirmed the defense verdict. The eight PREA reports about other complaints against the same officer are mentioned because the opinion mentions their admission; the brief says nothing about their contents, which the opinion does not describe.

applications.title: The line is scope and purpose, not force
applications.body: A clothed pat search, including the groin and waistband, can be required by legitimate security needs. It becomes an Eighth Amendment violation when the conduct exceeds what the security concern required and is done for the officer's gratification or to humiliate, degrade, or demean. No force and no injury are needed.

applications.title: Once it is a sexual assault, the usual defenses are gone
applications.body: The court presumes malice, rejects any injury requirement, and holds that the amount of force is irrelevant. Brief, over the clothing, and no harm are not defenses once a jury finds the touching was sexual.

applications.title: Say nothing about an inmate's body
applications.body: The remark "Is that all of you?" and the guards' laughter turned a search complaint into a sexual assault case. An officer's words during a search are evidence of purpose. Keep them to instructions.

applications.title: A witness who objects is a reason to slow down
applications.body: An inmate who said "that's not right" was "told to shut up," and that exchange reached the Ninth Circuit. Treat a bystander's objection as a reason to pause, bring in a second staff member, and document, not to silence the witness.

applications.title: Document the reason for an extended search the same day
applications.body: The defense in this case rested on a second officer's account of the waistband bulge, the investigator's report, and a demonstration of the search procedure. Record why the search went further, how long it took, who was present, and what was found. A PREA finding that the search was within policy did not end the lawsuit.

quiz.q: Under Bearchild v. Cobban, what must a prisoner prove to establish an Eighth Amendment violation based on sexual assault by staff?
options: That the staff member used significant physical force
That the prisoner suffered a physical or lasting emotional injury

That the staff member, without legitimate penological justification, touched the prisoner in a sexual manner or engaged in sexual conduct for the staff member's gratification or to humiliate, degrade, or demean the prisoner
That a PREA investigation substantiated the complaint
quiz.teach: That is the definition the court announced. No force and no injury are required, and once a sexual assault is proved, malicious and sadistic intent is presumed.

quiz.q: The search in Bearchild began as a pat-down on the way to a class. What did the court say a prisoner must show when the conduct began as a legitimate, invasive procedure?
options: That the search was not authorized by policy
That the guard's conduct exceeded the scope of what was required to satisfy the institutional concern that justified starting the procedure
That the search lasted more than one minute
That the guard had been the subject of prior complaints
quiz.teach: The court assumed legitimate penological objectives can require invasive searches. The question is whether the conduct went beyond what that concern required, for gratification or humiliation.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit decide about whether Sergeant Pasha sexually assaulted Bearchild?
options: It held that he did and entered judgment for Bearchild
It held that the search was lawful and affirmed the verdict
It decided nothing about what happened and ordered a new trial because the jury instruction misstated the elements
It held that qualified immunity barred the claim
quiz.teach: The court reversed for instructional error and remanded for a new trial. It made no finding on the facts, and the dissent would have affirmed the defense verdict.
